Republicans and Democrats clash for control across the country as midterms approach.

The 2026 midterm elections are just 100 days away, with both parties vying for control of Congress and statehouses. Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers, but Democrats need a net gain of just six House seats to reclaim the speaker's gavel and four Senate seats to win back the upper chamber.

In the House, Republicans will be bolstered by redistricting wins in states like Florida and Texas, while Democrats are focusing on the economy and affordability in their messaging. A recent Fox News poll showed that 53% of voters would back the Democratic candidate in their House district, a 7-point edge outside the margin of error.

In the Senate, Republicans are looking to hold on to seats in Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio, and Maine, with record amounts of spending already pouring into those states. Democrats hope to capitalize on the historic, economic, foreign policy, and anti-incumbent mood among voters.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from Fox News and The Guardian differ on the role of Donald Trump in the midterms. Fox News reports that Republicans are looking to tie Democrats to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in their midterm strategy, while The Guardian suggests that Trump's efforts to undermine the election process could have a significant impact on the outcome.

The accounts from Al Jazeera and BBC differ on the details of the Berlin Pride ramming attack. Al Jazeera reports that one person was killed and 17 injured, while BBC reports that one woman was killed and at least 29 others were injured.

Sources FOX News · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · NPR · BBC · Washington Examiner

US pauses strikes on Iran for third night as Trump weighs diplomatic options

The United States has paused its strikes on Iran for the third consecutive night, with President Donald Trump weighing his next move in the nearly five-month-old conflict. The pause follows a series of attacks and counterattacks between the two countries, which have resulted in dozens of deaths and significant damage to infrastructure.

According to reports, top military officials advised Trump to halt the bombing campaign due to dwindling munitions stockpiles that could hamper a sustained military campaign in the region. Diplomatic negotiations are ongoing to avoid a return to all-out war.

The Iranian army spokesperson announced on Sunday that Tehran had halted "retaliatory" attacks against US allies in the region, citing a pause in US strikes as the reason for this decision.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that President Trump said the U.S. has plenty of ammunition, following concerns about depleted stockpiles. However, The New York Post and Mother Jones report that administration officials have warned about dwindling munitions stockpiles that could hamper a sustained military campaign in the region.

The Christian Science Monitor and BBC report that Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks with Oman to manage the safe passage of ships on the Strait of Hormuz. However, The Guardian reports that Iranian officials have demanded payment and control over which ships pass through the strait.

Sources CBS News · Christian Science Monitor · Mother Jones · New York Post · BBC · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Three people killed and one suspect at large in Bite of Seattle food festival shooting

A shooting occurred on Sunday evening during the Bite of Seattle food festival at an events complex near the Space Needle in Seattle, Washington. According to authorities, three people were killed and four others, including a toddler, were wounded. One suspect was arrested, but another remains at large. Investigators believe the two suspects were shooting at each other.

The incident occurred around 6pm local time, when police and ambulances began responding to the scene. Two people died at the scene, and a third person died later at a hospital. The victims included two men, ages 19 and 44, and a 56-year-old woman. Four others were hospitalized, including a 2-year-old boy who was in stable condition.

Where the accounts differ

  • The accounts from various outlets differ in some details:
  • The Guardian reports that the shooting occurred at around 6pm local time, while FOX News reports it happened "shortly after 6 p.m."
  • Just The News and Al Jazeera report that one suspect surrendered at the scene, but FOX News does not mention this detail.
  • The Daily Wire reports that Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson lectured about "gun violence" during a press conference, but other outlets do not mention this.
  • The accounts from various outlets also differ in their descriptions of the victims and the injuries sustained.

Sources The Guardian · BBC · Just The News · The Daily Wire · Al Jazeera · FOX News

Mitch McConnell's prolonged absence stalls Senate legislation.

Mitch McConnell's extended absence from Washington, D.C., has stalled several legislative packages in the Senate. The party holds only a 53-to-47 majority in the Senate, making every vote critical. McConnell's absence, since a fall and subsequent hospitalization on June 14, has raised scrutiny from GOP colleagues worried about advancing bills before the deadline for the usual appropriations process on Oct. 1. If Congress does not pass the annual appropriations bill by Sept. 30, a partial government shutdown will ensue.

McConnell chairs the Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, making his voice a critical one on the panel, which has fallen into partisan deadlock due to his absence. The Appropriations Committee is split 14-14 between Democrats and Republicans, making it essentially impossible to advance controversial legislation. Senate Democrats have made it a negotiating tactic to not support advancing appropriations bills unless increases for the military are paired with similar increases for domestic programs.

The Agriculture Committee's work to advance the "farm bill," an omnibus, multiyear law that governs an array of agricultural and food programs, has also stalled, as McConnell is the second-ranking Republican on the panel. Republicans don't have enough votes without McConnell to advance it out of the Senate Agriculture Committee, since his absence leaves the panel at 11-11.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts conflict over the extent of McConnell's absence and its impact on legislation. The Washington Examiner reports that McConnell's absence has stalled high-stakes legislative packages, while FOX News notes that McConnell is still recovering from a medical emergency but has not provided a hard date for his return to Congress.

The New York Post quotes President Trump urging Senate Majority Leader John Thune to keep the chamber in session until it passes the SAVE America Act or ends the filibuster. However, The Hill reports that Thune has repeatedly pushed back on this demand by declaring there aren't nearly enough Republican votes to abolish the filibuster rule.

Newsweek provides a health update from Senator McConnell's doctor, stating that he is undergoing multiple physical therapy and rehabilitation sessions each day aimed at rebuilding strength and reducing the risk of future falls. However, the Washington Examiner reports that McConnell's absence has complicated sensitive negotiations to bring back an expired provision of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA).

Sources Washington Examiner · FOX News · New York Post · The Hill · Newsweek

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

Wildfires force over 300,000 people to evacuate homes in France and Spain.

Wildfires are raging across southwestern Europe, forcing more than 300,000 people to flee their homes. The blazes have burned vast areas of land in France and Spain, with authorities deploying thousands of firefighters to battle the fires. In France, over 220,000 people have been evacuated from their homes, while in Spain, around 75,000 people have been forced to leave.

The wildfires are among the worst in France since World War II, with some areas experiencing unprecedented heatwaves and droughts. The blazes have also affected the Tour de France, with the final stage of the cycling race being shortened due to the fires. In Spain, a fast-moving wildfire killed at least 12 people on July 10.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from different outlets conflict in several areas. NPR reports that over 250,000 people have been evacuated in France and Spain, while Al Jazeera states that more than 325,000 people have been forced to flee their homes. The Hill reports that no deaths have been tied to the fires, but CBS News mentions a person killed in the town of Manises in Spain.

NPR also provides specific numbers for the area burned by wildfires in France and Spain, stating that over 242,000 acres have been ravaged in France this year, while Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said that more than 300,000 acres have already burned in Spain. The Guardian reports that at least 240 homes in Gironde have been totally destroyed by the wildfire.

Sources NPR · BBC · The Hill · CBS News · The Guardian · Al Jazeera

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Federal appeals court rejects Trump bid to enforce mail ballot order ahead of midterm elections.

A federal appeals court on Saturday refused to let the Trump administration enforce key parts of President Donald Trump's executive order tightening mail-in voting rules in 23 Democratic-led states. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals denied the Department of Justice's request to pause a June ruling blocking several provisions of Trump's March executive order while the administration appeals. The court found that the plaintiff states were already facing looming election deadlines and had begun preparing for potential changes.

The lawsuit was brought by 23 states and the District of Columbia, led by California, Massachusetts, Nevada, and Washington. They argue that the Constitution gives them primary responsibility for administering federal elections and that the president exceeded his authority by directing federal agencies to impose new voting requirements. U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani agreed in June, ruling that several provisions of the executive order likely exceeded the president's authority and blocking federal agencies from implementing them in the plaintiff states through the Nov. 3 federal elections.

The Trump administration argued that the lawsuit was premature because federal agencies had not finalized the policies needed to implement the executive order. However, the appeals court rejected this argument, stating that the plaintiff states have no practical choice but to respond to the order now due to rapidly approaching deadlines.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News and The Hill report that the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals made a 2-1 decision, while Washington Examiner reports it as a "declined" request to lift an injunction. Just The News does not mention the vote count in its report. FOX News attributes criticism of the ruling to Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan, while The Hill mentions Trump's July primetime address on election integrity.

Sources FOX News · Washington Examiner · New York Post · Just The News · The Guardian · The Hill

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Dr. Anthony Fauci's diary entries reveal fixation on fame during COVID-19 pandemic.

Dr. Anthony Fauci's diary entries, released by Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), show a growing obsession with his public profile and media appearances as the COVID-19 pandemic raged on. The entries, spanning from December 2019 to December 2022, reveal Fauci's fixation on being in the spotlight, even as the death toll mounted worldwide.

Fauci's diary entries detail his interactions with President Donald Trump, governors, and world leaders, as well as his media appearances and personal observations during the pandemic. A recurring theme throughout the diaries is Fauci's growing awareness of his own public profile, which he described as "explosive and really unimaginable" by May 2020.

As the attention continued to grow, Fauci's diary entries documented how his prominence had expanded beyond public health. He noted that Secret Service agents had become so familiar with him they often waved him through White House security without checking his identification.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from The Daily Wire and New York Post report that Fauci wrote about being invited to appear on "Dancing with the Stars" in June 2020, while The Hill reports this invitation occurred a month later. The Federalist notes that CNN appears 275 times in Fauci's diary, while other outlets do not mention this specific detail.

The Guardian reports that Fauci described Trump as "rambling", "crazy", and "an idiot" in his diary entries, while other outlets focus on Fauci's fixation on fame. The Hill mentions that Fauci received a letter from Barbra Streisand expressing her appreciation for his guidance during the pandemic, but does not provide further details.

Sources The Daily Wire · New York Post · The Guardian · The Federalist · The Hill · FOX News

No source labeled lean-left or lean-right covered this story.

ICE To Target Haitians As Their Temporary Protected Status Expires

The US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is planning to target Haitian nationals whose Temporary Protected Status (TPS) is set to expire. Over 300,000 Haitians have been living in the US under TPS since 2010 due to turmoil in their home country. The Trump administration has argued that the program was never intended to be a permanent form of legal status.

The Supreme Court recently ruled in favor of the administration's efforts to terminate TPS for Haitians and Syrians, paving the way for ICE to begin enforcing deportations. According to internal documents obtained by CBS News, ICE plans to ramp up operations to arrest and deport Haitian migrants, with a focus on Ohio where large Haitian communities have been targeted by President Trump.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from The Daily Wire, The Guardian, FOX News, and CBS News all report that the TPS for Haitians is set to expire. However, there are some discrepancies in the numbers of Haitians affected: The Daily Wire reports 300,000, while The Guardian reports over 330,000.

Additionally, The Guardian attributes a characterization of the Trump administration's decision to end TPS as "racist" to Roxana Rivera, assistant to the president at Service Employees International Union (SEIU) 32BJ. This claim is not made by any other outlet.

The Daily Wire and CBS News both report that ICE plans to target Haitian migrants in Ohio, but The Guardian does not mention this specific detail.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Guardian · FOX News · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Cyclospora cases mounting in Michigan due to Trump admin cuts compromising food safety.

Cyclospora cases mounting in Michigan

Cyclospora cases have been reported in multiple states, including Michigan, where the outbreak is particularly severe. The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) has confirmed at least 7,400 cases of cyclospora, with many originating from Michigan and Ohio. State and local health officials are working to identify the cause of the outbreak, which may be linked to contaminated iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms in central Mexico.

The CDC has reported that cyclospora is generally transmitted through food or water contamination, rather than direct person-to-person contact. The parasite requires days or weeks to become infectious, making it difficult to track and contain outbreaks. In this case, the outbreak is believed to have originated from contaminated iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms.

The FDA has launched an investigation into the outbreak, which has affected nine states so far. Taylor Farms has recalled its products and temporarily suspended production at its central Mexico facility.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that there are over 11,000 cases of cyclospora reported in 41 states, while The Hill mentions a total of 7,400 confirmed cases. CBS News also quotes Susan Mayne as saying that the outbreak is "record-setting," which is not mentioned in The Hill's account.

Sources The Hill · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right or left or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

At least 1 dead, several injured after van rams into crowd at Pride festival

A white van rammed into a crowd of people attending a Pride festival in Berlin on Saturday evening, killing one person and injuring at least 16 others. The incident occurred during the European city's annual Christopher Street Day festival, an LGBTQ+ Pride event that attracts hundreds of thousands of people. Police said they have identified a suspect who is known to them and has links to "Islamic circles" in Berlin.

The attack happened around 10pm local time at Tiergarten Park, near the iconic Brandenburg Gate. The van crashed into a tree after hitting several people, and police later found the vehicle abandoned at the scene. Emergency services treated the injured, with some suffering life-threatening injuries.

Police launched an intensive manhunt for the suspect, who is believed to be armed and dangerous. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz condemned the incident as "a heinous act" on social media, saying that it was an attack on society's values of kindness and tolerance.

Where the accounts differ

  • The number of injured people reported by different outlets varies: 16 (FOX News), 17 (NPR), 29 (BBC).
  • The BBC reports that the suspect is a 21-year-old German citizen of Lebanese background, while other outlets do not provide this information.
  • The Washington Examiner mentions that police raided an apartment in connection with the investigation, but does not specify whether anyone was found there.

Sources FOX News · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · NPR · BBC · Washington Examiner

Trump delivers jokes and jabs at White House Correspondents' Association Dinner

President Donald Trump attended the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) Dinner on July 24, 2026, at the Waldorf Astoria hotel in Washington D.C. The event was originally scheduled for April but was disrupted by an assassination attempt on the president. Trump's speech included jokes and jabs at the press, politicians, and himself. He praised the Secret Service and law enforcement officers who responded to the April shooting, awarding Officer Victor Gonzales with the WHCA President's Award for Exceptional Service.

Trump also quipped about his relationship with the press, saying "sometimes I really do think that some of you don't like me." He joked that when he leaves office, the news industry will be "broke" because there won't be anyone to report on. Trump produced a "Trump 2028" hat and said he would run for a fourth term as president.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post reports that Trump mocked California Governor Gavin Newsom's 2028 White House ambitions, claiming Newsom had doomed himself with praise for Kamala Harris. The Guardian notes that Trump is reviving old tropes about communism and has identified it as the US's biggest threat.

FOX News highlights Trump's jokes at the press and members of his cabinet, including a quip about Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. cutting up a cow to bring beef tenderloin for dinner. The BBC reports that Trump took swipes at the press during the dinner, but also praised the Secret Service and law enforcement officers who responded to the April shooting.

The Hill notes that Trump's speech included a tribute to the U.S. Secret Service, law enforcement officers, and hotel staff who responded to the April incident. CBS News reports that Trump cracked jokes at reporters and politicians during the event, but also acknowledged the sometimes-tense relationship with the press.

Sources New York Post · FOX News · The Guardian · BBC · The Hill · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Maine Democrats crown Troy Jackson as Platner replacement as fresh scrutiny clouds Senate reset

Troy Jackson was elected as the Maine Democratic Party's nominee for U.S. Senate on Saturday at a nominating convention in Bangor. He will face Republican incumbent Susan Collins in November. Jackson, a former state Senate president and fifth-generation logger, won 566 of 571 delegate votes to secure the nomination.

The selection comes after Graham Platner dropped out of the race earlier this month due to allegations of sexual assault made by a former girlfriend. Platner denied the accusations but withdrew from the campaign.

Jackson's nomination caps an abbreviated process to find a replacement for Platner, who was backed by progressive champion and Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont. Jackson has been endorsed by Sanders in his past campaigns and supports progressive policies such as Medicare for All and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that there are concerns within the party about Jackson's alleged temper and workplace conduct, while NPR notes that these allegations have not led to significant public pushback from state leaders.

CBS News highlights the abbreviated process to find a replacement for Platner, which was triggered by his withdrawal from the race. The New York Post notes that many viewed Jackson as the favorite to succeed Platner due to his populist brand of politics.

The Daily Wire criticizes the Maine Democratic Party's decision-making process, suggesting that Jackson was hand-selected without a single vote being cast by Mainers.

Sources FOX News · NPR · CBS News · The New York Post · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Iran-backed Houthis claim missile attack on Saudi Arabia as regional tensions escalate

The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels claimed a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday, after vowing retaliation against the kingdom for attacks this week. The US and Iran have been engaged in a series of strikes over the past two weeks, with the US carrying out 13 consecutive nights of attacks on Iran. Iranian officials have publicly pushed back against US pressure while divisions persist inside Tehran over whether diplomacy or confrontation is the best path forward.

The Houthis said the attack was retaliation for Saudi airstrikes on Houthi targets in the Yemeni port city of Hodeida and a nearby island on Friday. The group had vowed to target ships attempting to transit the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The US military has fired on and disabled a tanker ship in the Gulf of Oman that was attempting to evade the American blockade on Iranian ports.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post reports that President Trump halted new US strikes on Iran as he weighs whether Tehran is ready to cut a deal, while the BBC states that there were no overnight reports of air strikes in the wider region by the US or Iran for the first time in two weeks. The Christian Science Monitor notes that the conflict is threatening to disrupt international shipping through the Red Sea.

Sources The Guardian · The Hill · New York Post · BBC · Christian Science Monitor · Just The News

More than 300,000 flee homes due to wildfires in France and Spain.

Wildfires have forced over 300,000 people to evacuate their homes in France and Spain. The fires have been burning for days, fueled by strong winds and high temperatures. In France, more than 167,000 people had been evacuated as of Saturday night, with the most devastating fires in the Southwest, particularly in the Gironde and Landes regions. French President Emmanuel Macron said that the situation remains critical in the Gironde department.

In Spain, at least one person has died from the fires, and over 60,000 people were evacuated from Avila and near Madrid. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared a national state of emergency due to the wildfires. The final stage of the Tour de France was shortened due to the fires, with security forces redeployed to assist with the response.

Where the accounts differ

  • NPR reports that over 242,000 acres have been burned in France this year, a historic record, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. The Guardian does not mention this specific figure.
  • The BBC quotes EU Commissioner for Crisis Management Hadja Lahbib as saying that last year one million hectares burned during the summer and they are expecting another historical record. This is also reported by NPR but not by other outlets.
  • CBS News reports that at least 197,000 people have been evacuated in France due to the wildfires, which French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said was "probably" the biggest peacetime evacuation the country has seen. The Guardian and BBC do not mention this specific figure.

Sources NPR · The Guardian · BBC · The Hill · CBS News · Al Jazeera

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

India's Education Minister Resigns Amid Nationwide Protests Over Exam Leaks and Education Reforms

India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday after weeks of protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth movement that has been demanding education reforms, compensation for families of students who died by suicide due to exam leaks, and accountability from the government. The protests began in May after allegations of leaks in some of India's biggest entrance exams.

The CJP, which started as a satirical campaign on social media, has grown into a powerful platform for young people's anxieties and dissent. Its founder, Abhijeet Dipke, rallied tens of thousands of students and supporters in New Delhi to force Pradhan's resignation. The movement has been marked by widespread protests, sit-ins, and hunger strikes across the country.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from different outlets highlight some differences in emphasis and reporting. NPR focuses on the government's shift in tactics and the role of Milan Vaishnav, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, who suggests that the government realized its usual playbook was not working. The Guardian emphasizes the significance of Pradhan's resignation as a major victory for the CJP and a challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's strongman image.

Sources NPR · The Guardian · BBC · Al Jazeera · Washington Examiner · CBS News

No source labeled right covered this story.

Federal appeals court rejects Trump bid to enforce key parts of mail-in voting order ahead of midterm elections.

A federal appeals court on Saturday refused to let the Trump administration enforce key parts of President Donald Trump's executive order tightening mail-in voting rules in 23 Democratic-led states. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to lift a lower-court injunction from June that ruled parts of the president's order was unconstitutional after Democratic-led states, including California, Massachusetts and Washington, sued the administration.

The appeals court rejected the administration's appeal in a 2-1 decision. The Trump order directed the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to compile lists of confirmed U.S. citizens eligible to vote and provide them to states, instructs the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) to establish new standards for mail-in ballots and directs the Justice Department to prioritize investigations into state and local election officials who issue federal ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote.

The lawsuit was brought by 23 states and the District of Columbia, led by California, Massachusetts, Nevada and Washington. The states argue the Constitution gives them primary responsibility for administering federal elections and that the president exceeded his authority by directing federal agencies to impose new voting requirements.

Where the accounts differ

  • FOX News and New York Post both report on Congressman Jim Jordan's criticism of the ruling, but only FOX News provides a quote from him.
  • The Hill reports on President Trump's July primetime address on election integrity, while The Guardian mentions his claims about widespread voter fraud in 2020.

Sources FOX News · Washington Examiner · New York Post · The Hill · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Israeli forces detain over 70 people in West Bank after deadly clashes between soldiers and Palestinian villagers.

At least four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers were killed in a shootout in the northern village of Tal in the occupied West Bank. The incident occurred when a group of about 20 Israeli settlers, many armed, approached the village with the intent to cause violence. Villagers confronted the settlers, and as tensions rose, Israeli soldiers arrived on the scene. A Palestinian man grabbed a gun from one of the settlers, leading to a shootout that resulted in the deaths of four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers.

The Israeli military confirmed that it had arrested more than 70 people across the West Bank overnight and into Saturday, with troops remaining in the village of Tell where the clashes erupted. The arrests were part of a wider crackdown on Palestinian residents, with reports of widespread searches and raids at hospitals and homes.

Where the accounts differ

The accounts from different outlets diverge in their descriptions of the events leading up to the shootout. The BBC reports that Palestinians confronted Jewish settlers who were attacking them, while Israel's military said it had responded to reports that hikers had been attacked. Al Jazeera states that a group of about 20 Israeli settlers approached the village with the intent to cause violence.

Sources The Hill · BBC · Al Jazeera

No source labeled left or right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: An 83-year-old man who went missing near the Grand Canyon was rescued after an overnight search.

Man, 83, who went missing near Grand Canyon rescued after overnight search

Gerald Guinn, an 83-year-old man from Utah, was hiking with another person in a remote location on the edge of the Kaibab National Forest at the Grand Canyon National Park. They split up to search for a nearby historic object, but Guinn never reunited with his companion. The other hiker searched for several hours before requesting help.

The Kane County Sheriff's Office Search and Rescue team conducted an overnight search using drones and search dogs, but found no sign of Guinn. The next morning, the Grand Canyon National Park Service took over the search efforts, adding a helicopter and ground teams to the search. A cell phone ping indicated Guinn's general location, leading the NPS to move the search to the east.

The NPS helicopter located Guinn, who was well enough to wave to the pilot. However, due to the terrain, the helicopter could not land, so a Kane County search and rescue team was sent to assess and stabilize Guinn.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that the operation was completed at 1:30 a.m., about a day and a half after Guinn first began his hike. FOX News does not provide this specific time frame.

Sources CBS News · FOX News

No source labeled center or lean-right or left covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Secret Service Increases Security for Rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association Dinner

The rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) dinner took place on July 24, 2026, at the Waldorf Astoria hotel in Washington D.C. The event was originally scheduled for April 25 but was postponed after an armed assailant attempted to assassinate President Donald Trump and other officials during the first dinner. Secret Service Director Sean Curran stated that the agency has seen a surge in threats against its protectees, with approximately 10,000 protective intelligence cases opened since January.

The rescheduled event featured enhanced security measures, including airport-style magnetometer screening for all ticketed guests, a visible police presence around the hotel, and traffic closures due to proximity to major thoroughfares. The Secret Service also implemented a separate entrance for guests rather than using the main lobby.

During the dinner, President Trump delivered a speech that included jokes at the expense of the press and his political opponents.
